extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel, corporate managers, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and professional standards for planning and executing public-relations/propaganda campaigns, including analysis, policy formulation, ethical limits, psychological methods, and tactics for influencing publics and opinion leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough client analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the client's product, markets, public reaction to the product, employees' attitudes toward the public and the product, and the cooperation of distribution agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel must study all phases of the client's activities that may affect the public. Examples: analyze an orphan asylum's organization to explain public indifference; inspect a manufacturer's product-market fit before attempting propaganda. This is the first step before any public-facing policy is set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough public analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the divisions of the public (social, economic, geographic, age, doctrinal, language, cultural groups) and identify the leaders through whom to approach these groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify group leaders and the particular groups that matter for the client's objectives; target approaches through those leaders rather than addressing every individual. Use this analysis to select media and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double analysis before policy formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct both the client analysis and the public analysis and collate the results prior to formulating policies governing the client's public contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after this double analysis should policies and procedures be drafted; these policies govern practice, procedure and habits in all public-facing aspects. Acting before agreement on policies risks wasted effort or harm to reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate public-facing policies before action
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and agree upon general policies governing the client's conduct in areas that affect the public before executing any campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should guide ongoing behavior (e.g., labor policy, customer service) as well as communications; some PR work ends once policies are set, while others require continuous implementation and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the product or idea is fundamentally sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid attempting to sell a fundamentally unsound or unmarketable product or idea; advise modification rather than deceptive promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is futile to promote something basically unsound. Example: advise orphan asylum reorganization to a 'cottage plan' if public expects that form; advise against trying to restore the corset but propose a healthier girdle alternative. If product cannot be made acceptable, refuse or decline to undertake the campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on product or organizational modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend concrete modifications to client practices, products or organization when analysis shows those changes are necessary for public acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: urging a railroad to run a prestige fast train to improve reputation; advising a company to reorganize an institution to fit modern sociological expectations. Counsel can and should propose structural solutions rather than only messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use leaders/influentials to influence the group
rubrics_metrics.description: Target and influence key leaders because influencing leaders (with or without their conscious cooperation) will influence their groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass psychology shows groups tend to follow trusted leaders. Practical tactic: invite famous or respected figures to events, or persuade professionals (e.g., physicians) to endorse practices to affect wide public behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage mass psychology and group characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Design campaigns based on the premise that the group mind operates by impulses, habits, emotions and cliches rather than individual rational deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cliches, pat words or images, associative symbols, and emotional currents to sway group opinion. Example: creating a new cliche (renaming 'evacuation hospitals') or applying existing cliches ('interests' or 'Bolshevik') to trigger automatic group responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create associative contexts and prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Use associative processes (events, exhibitions, architectural decisions, endorsements) to elevate an idea or product into a desirable social custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: staging a music-room exhibition with decorators and violinists to make owning a piano socially desirable; making a corporate building a landmark to carry associative prestige. The goal is to make the public 'own' the idea so demand appears to come from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contests, educational programs and institutional sponsorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage schoolchildren, professionals, and respected institutions in contests or programs that create grassroots interest and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ivory soap sculpture contests organized with art centers and schools stimulated productive activity, touched multiple motives (esthetic, competitive, maternal), and generated goodwill and product use across demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate varied communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the full range of media — conversation, letters, stage, motion pictures, radio, lectures, magazines, daily newspapers — selecting channels appropriate to the target groups and leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations is not the same as advertising; counsel should advocate advertising where appropriate but also use other channels and must coordinate them to present consistent information and manage perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement rather than duplicate advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate PR counsel work from advertising work; advocate advertising where indicated but avoid duplication of effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the counsel supplements the advertising agency's work; PR concentrates on public contacts and broader acceptance, while advertising typically addresses direct selling—both can collaborate synergistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and continuous monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the field systematically (clipping services, scouts, personal observation) to detect changes in taste, influential leaders, and issues; continuous monitoring is necessary because circumstances change unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR research is not an exact science; expect margins of error. Use the best available observation to predict effects (e.g., how an international flight may create goodwill) while recognizing unpredictable events can override plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilance and rumor management
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain constant vigilance and provide prompt, correct information through effective channels to stop rumors and suspicions at their source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single false rumor at a critical moment can have enormous financial consequences (e.g., driving down stock prices). Counsel should be in position to counteract misinformation promptly or establish relations of confidence so rumors fail to take root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label propaganda and maintain candor
rubrics_metrics.description: When sending out propaganda material, clearly label its source and purpose; be candid in dealings and avoid fooling or hoodwinking the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should know the source so they can judge material on its merits. A reputation for deception ends usefulness as a counsel. Candid labeling preserves long-term effectiveness and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and client selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse clients or causes believed to be dishonest, fraudulent, antisocial, hopeless, or in conflict with existing clients; counsel should apply an ethical code analogous to law or medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include preservation of reputation, inability to be dissociated from the client's acts in public opinion, and the long-term ineffectiveness of advocating manifestly bad causes. Don't accept clients with conflicting interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek overlapping, disinterested interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover points where the client's interests coincide with those of other individuals or groups to secure authentic cooperation from leaders and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders will lend authority only if the campaign touches something of real interest to them. Example: art educators sponsoring Ivory contests because it advanced esthetic education; railroads assisting chambers of commerce where interests align.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic events and ceremonies to dramatize ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage events (openings, ceremonies, exhibitions) timed and framed to maximize associative meaning and public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: timing a post office opening to coincide with a date important to postal history to create national interest; inviting prominent figures to add prestige and create newsworthy moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand unconscious motives behind actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Probe beyond stated reasons to underlying unconscious motives (e.g., status, exhibitionism, symbolic substitutes) to design persuasive appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freudian-influenced insights: people often act for compensatory substitutes. Effective propaganda addresses these hidden motives rather than only the rational explanations people give for their behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer removing sales resistance to direct assault
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than bluntly attacking competitors with repetitive direct appeals, create circumstances that reduce resistance and make adoption easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old-style repetition ('YOU buy X now') is less effective than setting up social currents and institutions (e.g., music rooms, exhibitions) that make people want to buy on their own initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professionals' endorsements strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and enlist professional authorities (e.g., physicians, artists, educators) whose public statements will influence mass behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: persuading physicians to publicly recommend bacon to shift dietary habits; using respected art centers and judges to legitimize consumer contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover and develop new markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PR to detect previously unsuspected markets and to promote growth that benefits both client and related communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: railroads developing communities along right-of-way, banks offering investment services to increase deposits, jewelry firms providing insurance to reduce buyer anxiety, baking companies offering recipes to expand bread uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the limits of predictive accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that propaganda and mass psychology have significant margins of error and are not exact sciences; plan with flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with good observation and tested principles, unexpected events or novel stimuli can change outcomes. The counsel should build contingencies and measure probable ranges of effect rather than claim certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether PR work is episodic or continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the counsel's work is limited (analysis and policy formulation) or requires ongoing communication to maintain public understanding and goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some campaigns end after analysis and policy changes; others require constant, frank information programs to sustain public appreciation and to counter continual misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid secrecy and excessive mystery in operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent an aura of secrecy about a corporation's dealings, because secrecy can breed suspicion and harm public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive in communicating honest, clear information about policies and operations; secrecy can act as an 'invisible drag' on a company's dealings with the public and financial markets.
